On top of that, "on-hold" state isn't explicitly mapped to any plan/act/verify category in the schema, and there's no definition of whether "duplicate type ID" is case-sensitive or how its scope is bounded.

Review this text only. Do not use tools or edit. Return exactly `verdict: pass|fail`, `findings: [...]`, `residual_risks: [...]`. PASS if no material planning decision is missing.

SCHEMA MODERNIZATION CONTRACT
Purpose: ticket features become specs. Ticket types are epic, bug, research, planning, implementation, review, interview, testing. Legacy types are task, feature, tracker-improvement.
Architecture: schemas use strict zero-or-one-parent linear inheritance. A universal work-item base defines lifecycle categories plan, act, verify. Each concrete type has at least one lifecycle path plan→act→verify and type-specific act work: epic orchestration; bug diagnosis/fix; research investigation; planning planning; implementation code change; review assessment; interview elicitation; testing execution. A lifecycle graph is the directed schema transition graph. A relation graph is ticket depends_on/linked edges. Derived schemas refine base category nodes into contained subgraphs. Nodes retain their inherited category. Edges are valid only within a category or across plan→act, act→verify, verify→act rework, act→plan replan. No skips. Per resolved schema graph, creation begins at exactly one plan root without inbound edges. Requests target concrete state nodes. Cancellation is a derived verify terminal leaf with no outgoing transition.
Registry: parent/cycle/duplicate validation is atomic at explicit load/reload; failure retains prior generation. Content hashes invalidate source descendants, resolved cache, manifest, catalog, and client version atomically. Typed manifest contains model_version, sources, schemas, graphs. Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas share primitives but declare local graphs. Built-in ticket schemas become JSON in Track 3. External/custom TOML and JSON are permanently supported by Track 2 with shared model parsing and parity fixtures. All eligible custom/built-in paths share one lexical sort. Any duplicate type ID, including built-in/custom collision, hard-fails the entire load and reports all paths lexically. Custom schemas cannot override built-ins.
Migration: Tracks are 1 engine/inheritance, 2 dual loader, 3 catalog/built-in JSON conversion, 4 clients, 5 migration, 6 validation. Bug/epic retain IDs and upgrade schemas/states in place. Active means open/planned/in-implementation/in-review/on-hold. Each active record needs direct lifecycle route or reviewer-selected typed remediation_approved_by relation to a review ticket with immutable approval decision; any missing proof blocks canonical upgrade and whole release. Pre-model active tickets are exempt until individual Track-5 migration. Current manifest rules apply on transition; pre-migration legacy tickets suspend all workflow checks; prior history is grandfathered. Task/tracker classifier research defines weights for six targets research/planning/implementation/review/interview/testing. Only unique top score >=0.80 auto-migrates; ties/lower/missing need approval. Immutable parts record classifier and approval. Feature: active child/dependency => epic; unchecked AC only => implementation; both => epic; neither => archived spec. Track 5 dry-runs and uses idempotent transactional batches, rolling back failed batch; latest approved decision wins; completion record ends Track 5. Track 6 blocks the whole release on any validation/repair failure, never rolls back completed batches/restores exemption, and starts forward transactional repair batches.
Evidence: unit/contract tests, CLI/MCP/HTTP parity, TOML/JSON resolved-manifest parity fixtures, migration dry-run/idempotence/rollback/live cutover/remediation tests, Playwright client tests, all-pass Track-6 matrix.

I'm reviewing this contract description for material gaps in planning decisions. Looking at the work item structure—the ticket types, inheritance model with plan/act/verify lifecycle, and how refinements nest within a single parent—I need to identify what critical planning elements might be missing or underspecified in the relation graph and overall governance model.

The next section covers registries, JSON/TOML handling, atomic operations, migration tracks, and how legacy tickets are grandfathered in as a cohort. I'm noting the classifier rules for research-driven weights, the deterministic feature migration table, and how Track 5 and Track 6 handle transactional batches and release blocking—these are the operational constraints that shape how the contract actually executes.

Now I'm checking for gaps in the design. The cancellation logic is consistent, the classifier boundary between task/tracker and epic/bug holds up, but there's a critical missing piece: if Track 6's corrective migration batch fails again, there's no specified retry limit or escalation path. The current spec says "never rollback" and "launches idempotent transactional corrective migration batch from current state," but that could create an infinite loop if the corrective batch itself keeps failing. That's a material gap—I need a termination condition or escalation strategy there. The approval path for the classifier is also underspecified, though that might be out of scope.

The verdict is that this fails, primarily because of that missing failure-loop termination for Track 6, plus the residual risks that creates.

arguments.title: Tracker: schema lifecycle inheritance and phased migration
arguments.description:
## Objective

Deliver the resolved ticket-schema modernization program: inherited lifecycle schemas, directed lifecycle graphs, dual-format external schemas, a safe legacy migration, and release validation.

## Governing Decisions

- Features are represented by specs, not ticket types.
- New work-item ticket types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`; `task`, `feature`, and `tracker-improvement` are legacy pending migration.
- Schemas use strict zero-or-one-parent linear inheritance from a universal work-item schema with `plan`, `act`, and `verify` lifecycle categories. Every concrete type must provide a valid path through all three; its `act` is type-specific.
- A `lifecycle graph` governs directed schema state transitions. A `relation graph` governs ticket edges such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and `remediation_approved_by`; relation edges have no category constraint.
- Child schemas refine inherited lifecycle nodes into category-contained subgraphs. Legal cross-category lifecycle edges are `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`, `verify -> act` for rework, and `act -> plan` for replanning. No ordinary category skips. Creation starts at the unique plan-category root per resolved schema graph.
- Cancellation is a derived verify-category terminal leaf. It is the explicit exception that may be entered directly from any category; terminal nodes have no outgoing lifecycle edges.
- Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse the shared directed primitives but retain separate type-ID namespaces and local lifecycle graphs.
- Built-in ticket schemas convert to JSON. Custom schema directories permanently accept TOML and JSON through a shared model parser. Any type-ID collision, including built-in/custom, rejects the entire load. Diagnostics sort the combined eligible path union lexically and report every collision.
- Explicit reload atomically updates the registry generation, resolved-schema cache, manifest/catalog, and client cache version; failure preserves the prior generation. The typed manifest contains `model_version`, `sources`, `schemas`, and `graphs`.
- `bug` and `epic` keep canonical IDs and upgrade schemas/states in place. For active tickets (`open`, `planned`, `in-implementation`, `in-review`, `on-hold`), a direct lifecycle route or a reviewer-selected `remediation_approved_by` relation to an approved immutable review decision is required; otherwise the type upgrade and release are blocked. Pre-model active tickets are exempt pending individual migration.
- All pre-cutover legacy tickets are one exempt cohort: workflow checks suspend until each ticket is migrated by a committed approved Track-5 batch; old history is grandfathered and the next transition uses the current manifest.
- The rules-first classifier applies only to legacy `task` and `tracker-improvement`. Only a unique top score at least 0.80 auto-migrates; tied, lower, or missing scores require a linked review-ticket decision. Legacy `feature` uses the deterministic feature-to-spec mapping described in Track 5.
- Track 5 batches are idempotent and transactional. Track 6 blocks the entire release on any validation or forward-repair failure, never rolls back committed batches, and uses corrective transactional migrations. Corrective evidence is an immutable `corrective-migration` part superseding the original; the latest approved superseding decision is authoritative. One corrective retry is allowed; a second failure needs a human-approved remediation review.

## Validation

Each track requires focused unit and contract tests. Exposed behavior requires CLI/MCP/HTTP parity. Dual-format fixture pairs compare resolved manifests. Migration validation covers dry run, idempotence, failed-batch rollback, live cutover, approval authorization, and corrective migration. Client changes require Playwright coverage. Track 6 requires the full matrix to pass before release.

## Track Order

1. Engine and inheritance
2. Dual-format loader
3. Generated catalog and built-in JSON conversion
4. CLI and VS Code clients
5. Legacy migration
6. Cross-interface release validation

## Objective

Deliver the resolved ticket-schema modernization program: inherited lifecycle schemas, directed lifecycle graphs, dual-format external schemas, a safe legacy migration, and release validation.

## Governing Decisions

- Features are represented by specs, not ticket types.
- New work-item ticket types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`; `task`, `feature`, and `tracker-improvement` are legacy pending migration.
- Schemas use strict zero-or-one-parent linear inheritance from a universal work-item schema with `plan`, `act`, and `verify` lifecycle categories. Every concrete type must provide a valid path through all three; its `act` is type-specific.
- A `lifecycle graph` governs directed schema state transitions. A `relation graph` governs ticket edges such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and `remediation_approved_by`; relation edges have no category constraint.
- Child schemas refine inherited lifecycle nodes into category-contained subgraphs. Legal cross-category lifecycle edges are `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`, `verify -> act` for rework, and `act -> plan` for replanning. No ordinary category skips. Creation starts at the unique plan-category root per resolved schema graph.
- Cancellation is a derived verify-category terminal leaf. It is the explicit exception that may be entered directly from any category; terminal nodes have no outgoing lifecycle edges.
- Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse the shared directed primitives but retain separate type-ID namespaces and local lifecycle graphs.
- Built-in ticket schemas convert to JSON. Custom schema directories permanently accept TOML and JSON through a shared model parser. Any type-ID collision, including built-in/custom, rejects the entire load. Diagnostics sort the combined eligible path union lexically and report every collision.
- Explicit reload atomically updates the registry generation, resolved-schema cache, manifest/catalog, and client cache version; failure preserves the prior generation. The typed manifest contains `model_version`, `sources`, `schemas`, and `graphs`.
- `bug` and `epic` keep canonical IDs and upgrade schemas/states in place. For active tickets (`open`, `planned`, `in-implementation`, `in-review`, `on-hold`), a direct lifecycle route or a reviewer-selected `remediation_approved_by` relation to an approved immutable review decision is required; otherwise the type upgrade and release are blocked. Pre-model active tickets are exempt pending individual migration.
- All pre-cutover legacy tickets are one exempt cohort: workflow checks suspend until each ticket is migrated by a committed approved Track-5 batch; old history is grandfathered and the next transition uses the current manifest.
- The rules-first classifier applies only to legacy `task` and `tracker-improvement`. Only a unique top score at least 0.80 auto-migrates; tied, lower, or missing scores require a linked review-ticket decision. Legacy `feature` uses the deterministic feature-to-spec mapping described in Track 5.
- Track 5 batches are idempotent and transactional. Track 6 blocks the entire release on any validation or forward-repair failure, never rolls back committed batches, and uses corrective transactional migrations. Corrective evidence is an immutable `corrective-migration` part superseding the original; the latest approved superseding decision is authoritative. One corrective retry is allowed; a second failure needs a human-approved remediation review.

## Validation

Each track requires focused unit and contract tests. Exposed behavior requires CLI/MCP/HTTP parity. Dual-format fixture pairs compare resolved manifests. Migration validation covers dry run, idempotence, failed-batch rollback, live cutover, approval authorization, and corrective migration. Client changes require Playwright coverage. Track 6 requires the full matrix to pass before release.

## Track Order

1. Engine and inheritance
2. Dual-format loader
3. Generated catalog and built-in JSON conversion
4. CLI and VS Code clients
5. Legacy migration
6. Cross-interface release validation

arguments.body:
<!-- aligned-structure:v2 -->

## Motivation
Ticket schemas are duplicated, transitions are currently undirected, and schema loading cannot express the planned work-item hierarchy safely. This contract establishes directed lifecycle graphs, runtime inheritance, compatible TOML/JSON schema loading, and an auditable migration path.

## Dependent Expectation
If implemented, ticket, spec, and rule schema consumers can resolve an inherited schema deterministically, validate directed lifecycle transitions, and migrate legacy ticket records without losing an auditable transition history.

## Guards
Guards will be recorded by the linked implementation tracks before review: resolver contracts, loader parity fixtures, migration dry-run/idempotence/cutover checks, transport parity, and browser checks for client changes.

## Positions
- `memory-api/crates/memory-api/src/model/schema.rs`: partial; flat state strings and undirected transitions.
- `memory-api/crates/ticket-api/src/model/schema_registry.rs`: partial; flat TOML-only registry with replacement semantics.
- `memory-api/crates/ticket-api/schemas/`: partial; duplicated built-in workflows.
- `memory-api/tools/cli/ticket-cli`: partial; default type is legacy `tracker-improvement`.
- `memory-api/tools/ticket-vscode`: partial; type picker is hard-coded to `tracker-improvement`.

## Contract
- Features are spec-owned. Ticket types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`; `task`, `feature`, and `tracker-improvement` are legacy until migration.
- Schemas use strict single-parent inheritance from a universal work-item lifecycle. Resolved lifecycle graphs use `plan`, `act`, and `verify` categories; every concrete type has a valid path through all three.
- Lifecycle graphs are directed schema transitions. Relation graphs are ticket links and have no lifecycle-category constraints.
- TOML and JSON custom schemas have identical semantics. Shipped ticket built-ins convert to JSON; any duplicate type ID in the same schema-kind registry hard-fails atomic load/reload.
- Legacy migration is transactional, auditable, and forward-repairable. Ambiguous classification requires a linked review-ticket decision.

## Governing-Rule Requirement
A policy rule introducing this spec and the validation guards must be added or linked by the implementation tracks before the spec is treated as implemented.

## Objective
Implement the schema-modernization contract established in [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml).

## Decision Record
- Features are owned by specs; the new work-item types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`.
- Runtime schemas use strict single-parent inheritance and directed lifecycle graphs. Relation graphs remain separate ticket-edge graphs.
- Work-item lifecycle categories are `plan`, `act`, and `verify`; each concrete type must provide a path through all three.
- Shipped ticket schemas move to JSON; custom TOML and JSON remain supported with identical semantics. Type IDs are unique per schema kind; every collision is a full atomic-load error.
- Legacy records migrate through approved, idempotent transactional batches. Track 6 repairs only forward; it never reverts committed batches.

## Child Tracks
1. Engine and inheritance semantics
2. Dual-format schema loader
3. Resolved catalog and JSON built-ins
4. CLI and VS Code integration
5. Inventory and transactional migration
6. Cross-interface validation and release gate

arguments.title: Implement directed inherited schema lifecycle engine
arguments.description:
## Objective
Implement the shared directed schema engine required by [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml).

## Requirements
- Add strict linear zero-or-one-parent inheritance with atomic full-load/reload validation for missing parents and cycles.
- Resolve child lifecycle graphs as category-contained refinements of universal `plan`, `act`, and `verify` nodes.
- Require exactly one plan-category root per resolved schema and a valid path through all categories for each concrete work-item type.
- Enforce directed lifecycle edges: same category, `plan→act`, `act→verify`, `verify→act`, and `act→plan`; reject skips.
- Keep lifecycle graphs distinct from relation graphs; ticket/spec/rule registries reuse primitives but keep separate schema-kind namespaces and local graphs.
- Make `cancelled` a derived verify terminal leaf; terminal nodes have no outgoing edge.
- Explicit reload atomically swaps registry generation, resolved caches, manifest/catalog index, and client cache version, or retains the prior valid generation.

## Acceptance Criteria
Focused tests prove directionality, inheritance resolution, category containment, terminal validation, atomic reload rollback, and cache invalidation across ancestor changes.

arguments.title: Add deterministic dual-format schema loading
arguments.description:
## Objective
Extend schema loading for the contract in [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml).

## Requirements
- Parse external/custom `.toml` and `.json` schemas into the same model with identical inheritance and validation semantics.
- Sort the combined set of eligible TOML and JSON paths lexically before parsing and diagnostics.
- Treat every duplicate `type_id` in the same schema-kind registry, including built-in/custom collisions, as a complete atomic-load failure; report all colliding paths in lexical order.
- Preserve the previous valid registry generation when a reload fails.
- Add TOML/JSON fixture pairs that compare resolved-manifest output.

## Acceptance Criteria
Tests cover mixed-format success, cross-format collisions, multi-file collisions, invalid JSON/TOML diagnostics, deterministic ordering, and prior-generation retention.

arguments.title: Generate resolved schema catalog and JSON built-ins
arguments.description:
## Objective
Replace shipped ticket-schema TOML sources with generated JSON built-ins backed by the resolved registry manifest in [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml).

## Requirements
- Convert all shipped ticket built-ins (`tracker-improvement`, `task`, `feature`, `bug`, `epic`) to JSON and delete shipped TOML copies only after the dual loader passes.
- Generate a typed resolved-registry manifest with model version, source hashes, parent chains, resolved hashes, nodes, transitions, terminals, type metadata, and local graph membership.
- Define new concrete work-item schema types: `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, `testing`.
- Ensure every concrete type refines the universal lifecycle and has an explicit path through plan, act, and verify. `epic` act means orchestration; `bug` act means diagnosis/fix.

## Acceptance Criteria
Generated artifacts are reproducible, manifest schema is validated, built-ins load as JSON, external TOML remains accepted, and every concrete lifecycle passes graph validation.

arguments.title: Integrate schema catalog into CLI and VS Code
arguments.description:
## Objective
Replace hard-coded legacy ticket-type choices with catalog-driven client behavior.

## Requirements
- Update ticket CLI creation defaults and type selection using the resolved registry catalog.
- Update the VS Code ticket extension picker, commands, and validation to consume catalog-provided types.
- Surface lifecycle transition guidance from the resolved lifecycle graph.
- Reload cache versions coherently after atomic registry generation changes.

## Acceptance Criteria
CLI, MCP, and HTTP behavior agree on types and transitions. VS Code browser/client coverage proves the updated type picker and transition workflow. No client may silently select an unavailable schema type.

arguments.title: Inventory and migrate legacy ticket schemas
arguments.description:
## Objective
Inventory and migrate legacy `task`, `feature`, `tracker-improvement`, and upgraded `bug`/`epic` records safely.

## Requirements
- Produce a type/state inventory before migration.
- Treat all pre-model legacy records as one workflow-exempt cohort until individually migrated; grandfather prior history.
- For active bug/epic records (`open`, `planned`, `in-implementation`, `in-review`, `on-hold`), require either a direct lifecycle route or a reviewer-selected `remediation_approved_by` relation to an immutable review decision; missing proof blocks that canonical upgrade and the release.
- Classify `task`/`tracker-improvement` only through a rules-first research sub-ticket. Only a unique score ≥0.80 auto-migrates; tied, lower, or missing scores require a linked review-ticket decision.
- Migrate legacy `feature` records deterministically: active child/dependency -> epic; unchecked acceptance criterion only -> implementation; both -> epic; neither -> archived spec.
- Use idempotent transactional batches. Persist immutable migration parts. A committed approved batch removes the individual exemption.

## Acceptance Criteria
Dry-run, idempotence, batch rollback, remediation authorization, classifier approval, feature conversion, and live-cutover tests pass. The exact inventory and decisions are auditable.

arguments.title: Validate schema modernization release and repair flow
arguments.description:
## Objective
Provide the release gate and forward-repair protocol for schema modernization.

## Requirements
- Require focused unit/contract checks, CLI/MCP/HTTP parity, TOML/JSON resolved-manifest fixtures, migration dry-run/idempotence/rollback/live-cutover/remediation checks, and Playwright client coverage.
- Track 6 blocks the entire release on any failed validation or forward-repair batch.
- Never roll back committed migration batches or restore a legacy exemption after migration completion.
- On failure, run one transactional corrective migration batch from current state. If the retry fails, keep release blocked and require a linked human-approved remediation review ticket.
- Preserve original immutable migration evidence. Corrective work appends an immutable `corrective-migration` part linked by `supersedes`; the latest approved superseding part is authoritative.

## Acceptance Criteria
The validation matrix is executable and release-blocking. Corrective migration, retry cap, review escalation, immutable evidence chaining, and repair-forward behavior have automated tests.

tool_arguments_json.title: Validate schema modernization release and repair flow
tool_arguments_json.description:
## Objective
Provide the release gate and forward-repair protocol for schema modernization.

## Requirements
- Require focused unit/contract checks, CLI/MCP/HTTP parity, TOML/JSON resolved-manifest fixtures, migration dry-run/idempotence/rollback/live-cutover/remediation checks, and Playwright client coverage.
- Track 6 blocks the entire release on any failed validation or forward-repair batch.
- Never roll back committed migration batches or restore a legacy exemption after migration completion.
- On failure, run one transactional corrective migration batch from current state. If the retry fails, keep release blocked and require a linked human-approved remediation review ticket.
- Preserve original immutable migration evidence. Corrective work appends an immutable `corrective-migration` part linked by `supersedes`; the latest approved superseding part is authoritative.

## Acceptance Criteria
The validation matrix is executable and release-blocking. Corrective migration, retry cap, review escalation, immutable evidence chaining, and repair-forward behavior have automated tests.

1. **High**: Lifecycle validation lacks explicit per-category entry semantics, resolved-node reachability, illegal category-escape checks, and test obligations for the permitted rework/replan loops. The engine ticket only requires one `plan` root and allowed edge classes.

   Record change: add the full validator contract and acceptance tests for one entry per resolved category, terminal semantics, reachability, containment/tunnel boundaries, illegal escapes, and permitted loops.

2. **High**: The validation/release track does not identify viewers, search, or indexing as applicable schema consumers, nor provide acceptance evidence for those surfaces. “Playwright client coverage” is too broad to establish cross-client compatibility.  
   Owner: [3bb41fb2 Validate schema modernization release and repair flow](.ticket/tickets/3bb41fb2-9907-4b54-83b1-c62a0ce96756/ticket.toml).  
   Record change: add an interface matrix naming CLI, MCP, HTTP, VS Code, each affected viewer, and search/indexing; attach an executable validation obligation or an explicit justified non-applicability decision for each.

3. **High**: State, type, lifecycle category, relation, and validation-gate remain insufficiently separated as model concepts. The spec separates lifecycle and relation graphs, but does not define the five-way distinction or validation boundaries.  
   Owner: [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml), implemented by [7ef3f8db Implement directed inherited schema lifecycle engine](.ticket/tickets/7ef3f8db-d4a9-4135-99eb-3c006070a328/ticket.toml).  
   Record change: add a glossary/invariants section and engine acceptance tests that reject conflating categories with states/types, lifecycle edges with relations, or validation gates with lifecycle nodes.

4. **Medium**: Category-contained refinement is recorded, but the contained subgraph/tunnel entry-and-exit semantics from the interview are not explicit.  
   Owner: [7ef3f8db Implement directed inherited schema lifecycle engine](.ticket/tickets/7ef3f8db-d4a9-4135-99eb-3c006070a328/ticket.toml).  
   Record change: define refinement as a contained subgraph with explicit permitted boundary transitions and tests proving derived nodes cannot bypass the parent-category tunnel.

5. **Medium**: Lifecycle and relation graphs are recorded as separate, but the relation/dependency graph’s required non-lifecycle directionality is not stated.  
   Owner: [e9c38d24 Schema modernization lifecycle and migration](.spec/specs/e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f/spec.toml).  
   Record change: explicitly define relation/dependency graph semantics and state that lifecycle direction/category validation never applies to relation edges.

6. **Medium**: Dual-format loading specifies TOML/JSON parity, ordering, and atomic collision handling, but does not expressly make external TOML and JSON support permanent.  
   Owner: [1f8e6e6d Add deterministic dual-format schema loading](.ticket/tickets/1f8e6e6d-c8ea-461d-83c9-c26daf0e3cd3/ticket.toml).  
   Record change: state permanent compatibility as a non-removal guarantee and add a regression obligation preserving mixed-format external loads after built-in JSON conversion.

7. **Medium**: Catalog-driven client behavior requires replacing hard-coded choices, but the acceptance criteria do not prove removal or a defined compatibility adapter for each legacy list.  
   Owner: [9e7a5f1a Integrate schema catalog into CLI and VS Code](.ticket/tickets/9e7a5f1a-a2ce-43ce-9c8f-bdce7cf712d2/ticket.toml).  
   Record change: enumerate legacy type-list call sites, require their deletion or named adapter, and add regression tests proving catalog changes alter CLI and VS Code selection without source-list drift.

**Decision questions requiring user judgement**

None. The transcript resolves the missing behavior; the gaps are record and validation omissions, not unresolved product choices.

**Handoff readiness:** blocked. The ordered dependency chain is correct, but the seven findings leave lifecycle validation, concept boundaries, client-surface coverage, and permanent format compatibility insufficiently traceable for implementation planning.

content.objective: Implement the schema lifecycle engine slice that enforces strict zero-or-one-parent inheritance and directed lifecycle graphs (categories: plan/act/verify) with contained refinement tunnels, explicit root/entry/terminal/reachability/loop validation, separation of lifecycle graph from ticket-relation graph, atomic reload/generation + cache invalidation, and comprehensive unit/property tests that prevent conflation of type/state/category/relation/validation-gate.
decisions: Canonical representation for parent relation: enforce Option<ParentId> with API that prevents setting a second parent (policy + type-level invariant).
Lifecycle graph model: explicit typed node categories (`Plan | Act | Verify`) with typed edges; refinement tunnels are typed, bounded subgraphs rather than ad-hoc edges.
Validation contract: define and implement explicit validators for root/entry/terminal, reachability, and loop detection; validators run in compile-time/unit-test harness and at reload time.
Graph vs ticket-relation separation: lifecycle graph stored/serialized independently from ticket relation graph; tickets reference lifecycle node ids but do not embed graph structure.
Atomic reload strategy: generation produces a versioned artifact + atomic swap of in-memory reference; cache invalidation via generation version bump and single-writer lock-free handoff pattern.

Testing approach: combine focused unit tests, property-based tests for invariants (no >1 parent, no cycles, reachability), and deterministic fixtures to prevent conflation of type/state/category/relation/validation-gate.
Error model and migration policy: choose fail-fast on invariant violation during reload (reject generation) vs best-effort repair — decision required if migration/repair belongs downstream.
validation: Unit test: enforce zero-or-one-parent invariant (attempt to set second parent must error) for `schema.rs` model constructors and setters.
Graph validation tests: detect cycles, unreachable nodes, missing root/entry/terminal nodes for representative graphs; tests must exercise positive and negative cases.

Category separation tests: assert nodes carry explicit category (`Plan|Act|Verify`) and that validators enforce allowed edge patterns (e.g., Plan -> Act allowed, Verify -> Plan disallowed where specified).
Refinement tunnel tests: construct refinement tunnels and assert containment, entry/exit invariants, and that refinement does not leak edges that violate lifecycle categories.
Separation tests: unit tests proving lifecycle graph serialization/deserialization is decoupled from ticket relation graph, and tickets reference lifecycle node ids only.

Atomic reload tests: simulate concurrent readers during generation; verify that reload yields either old or new consistent graph (no partial state), and that cache invalidation/version bump is observed by clients.

Negative/regression tests: ensure tests exist that would have caught conflations (type vs state vs category vs relation vs validation-gate) — include fixture cases that previously caused misclassification.

Integration smoke tests (local, limited): run focused tests adjacent to crates to confirm compilation and the new invariants do not break crate build (loader/catalog integration is out-of-scope but ensure compile-time contracts remain stable).
non_goals: Loader/catalog/clients/migration/release workflows (these are downstream and out of scope for this unit).
UI, viewer, or external deployment automation for schema releases.
Database migration execution or cross-service rollout logic.
Broad refactor of unrelated schema tooling or rewriting unrelated crates.

context_anchors.evidence_notes: Independent Review Agent passed the planning track with zero findings and ticket-health scoped to the epic reports zero findings.

risk_notes: Ambiguity risk: incomplete prior decisions about migration/repair vs reject-on-invalid-generation can cause downstream rework; requires explicit policy before integrating with loader/migration.
Backward-compatibility risk: changes to schema representation or node ids may break downstream loader/catalog consumers — guard via versioned generation and compatibility shims.
Concurrency risk: incorrect reload/invalidation design may allow readers to see partial state; rigorous atomic-swap tests are required.
Test fragility risk: property tests must be deterministic; flaky random-seed tests could mask regressions—pin seeds or use shrinking with repeatable harness.
Scope creep risk: adding loader/catalog work into this slice will broaden test surface and block delivery; keep strict slice boundaries.
content.next_after: After implementing and landing the lifecycle engine unit+tests, the next step is to implement the loader/registry and migration integration (downstream): wire generation/versioning to the loader, expand integration tests across registry/clients, and add end-to-end migration/release validation.

arguments.content:
# Ticket Schema Modernization Interview

This file records the full interview conducted after the initial review of
[input.clean.md](input.clean.md). Entries are chronological. A decision marked
**Superseded** was replaced by a later answer and is not part of the final
planning contract.

## Final Planning Contract

- Feature functionality is represented by specs, not ticket types.
- New work-item ticket types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`,
  `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`.
- `task`, `feature`, and `tracker-improvement` are legacy ticket types until
  their individual Track 5 migrations.
- Schemas use strict, runtime, single-parent inheritance beneath a universal
  work-item schema. Resolved schemas are dynamically generated and cached.
- The universal work-item lifecycle categories are `plan`, `act`, and
  `verify`. Every concrete work-item type refines one or more nodes in each
  category and has at least one valid path across all three categories.
- A schema's directed state-transition structure is the **lifecycle graph**.
  Ticket links such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and
  `remediation_approved_by` form the **relation graph**.
- Derived schemas refine inherited lifecycle nodes into category-contained
  subgraphs. A resolved node retains the inherited category label. Edges may
  remain within a category or cross only between neighbouring category edges:
  `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`, `verify -> act` for rework, and
  `act -> plan` for replanning. No normal lifecycle skips are permitted.
- Each resolved work-item schema has exactly one plan-category root with no
  inbound lifecycle edge; creation begins there. Every transition names a
  concrete target state and is validated against the resolved lifecycle graph.
- Cancellation is a derived `verify` terminal leaf. It is the sole exception
  that may be reached directly from any lifecycle category. Terminal nodes
  have no outgoing edges.
- Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse shared directed lifecycle
  primitives while maintaining separate local graphs and separate type-ID
  namespaces.
- Schema inheritance is linear: zero or one parent; missing parents and cycles
  are rejected. Parent/cycle/type-ID validation occurs during an explicit,
  atomic load or reload. A failed reload retains the last valid registry.
- On explicit reload, source and ancestor content hashes invalidate affected
  resolved-schema cache entries, resolved manifests, catalog indexes, and
  client cache versions atomically.
- The typed resolved-registry manifest includes `model_version`, `sources`,
  `schemas`, and `graphs`. Schema records include IDs, parent chains, hashes,
  resolved nodes, transitions, terminals, and type metadata. Graph records
  name their entity kind and schema IDs.
- Shipped ticket schemas become JSON sources. External/custom schema directories
  permanently support both TOML and JSON through a shared model/parser.

11. **Question:** Where should global directed transition/category migration
    live?

12. **Question:** Can a ticket return from verification to work for rework?
    **Answer:** Yes: explicit `verify -> act -> verify` lifecycle loop.

13. **Question:** How should legacy schemas be handled by the global engine?
    **Answer:** Initially selected exemption from category enforcement until
    type migration. **Final:** the whole pre-cutover legacy cohort suspends
    workflow checks until individual migration.

14. **Question:** Who produces TOML and JSON artifacts?

    built-ins plus permanently supported custom TOML/JSON inputs.

15. **Question:** Should duplicate diagnostics list every collision?
    **Answer:** Yes, all colliding paths in lexical order.

16. **Question:** How should `review` type be distinguished from lifecycle
    category?

17. **Question:** Are epics exempt from the universal lifecycle?
    **Answer:** No. An epic traverses all categories; its `act` is orchestration
    and dependency coordination.

19. **Question:** How does directed enforcement apply to historical legacy
    transitions?

    `model_version` cutover. Old history is unchanged and grandfathered.

20. **Question:** Does Track 5 execute live migration?
    **Answer:** Yes. Track 5 inventories, maps, dry-runs, executes idempotent
    transactional batches, removes exemptions, and writes a completion record.

21. **Question:** How do migrated legacy records satisfy universal lifecycle
    evidence?
    **Answer:** Their pre-cutover history is grandfathered; subsequent
    transitions follow the new rules.

22. **Question:** What is the required track order?
    **Answer:** Final sequence: engine/inheritance, dual loader, catalog and
    shipped JSON conversion, clients, migration, validation.

23. **Question:** Are shipped built-ins all converted before conversion
    cutover?
    **Answer:** Yes. Every shipped ticket built-in is converted to JSON;
    built-in TOML sources are deleted in catalog/conversion work.

24. **Question:** What happens to existing `bug` and `epic` IDs?
    **Answer:** Retain IDs and upgrade their schemas and active states in place,
    subject to global preflight.

25. **Question:** Does the directed engine apply only to tickets?
    **Answer:** No. Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse shared
    directed primitives but define local lifecycle graphs.

26. **Question:** Which rule schemas are included?
    **Answer:** Existing rule-api schemas such as `rule-entry` and
    `generated-target`; no new rule entity is introduced.

27. **Question:** When must the dual loader exist relative to shipped TOML
    deletion?
    **Answer:** The dual loader lands before built-in TOML sources are deleted.

28. **Question:** How should external custom TOML schemas work?
    **Answer:** They remain permanently supported alongside custom JSON.

29. **Question:** May custom schemas override built-ins?
    **Answer:** No. Any collision, including built-in/custom, is fatal.

30. **Question:** What is the duplicate-ID namespace?
    **Answer:** Type IDs are unique per schema kind; ticket, spec, and rule
    registries have separate namespaces.

### Runtime inheritance and lifecycle graph decisions

31. **Question:** Should inheritance return to the design?
    **Answer:** Yes. Runtime inheritance resolves derived schemas dynamically
    and caches unchanged resolved schemas for low-latency use.

32. **Question:** What parent topology is allowed?
    **Answer:** Strict zero-or-one parent, linear parent chains only; missing
    parents and cycles fail.

33. **Question:** How should derived states relate to base lifecycle states?
    **Answer:** A derived schema refines inherited lifecycle nodes into contained
    subgraphs or tunnels. Resolved nodes retain inherited base-category labels.

34. **Question:** How does a transition enter a derived category tunnel?
    **Answer:** A transition explicitly names a concrete target state; the
    resolver validates the resolved concrete edge and inherited category pair.

35. **Question:** How should child state-object overrides work?
    **Answer:** Earlier field-wise merge and explicit entry-flag options were
    **superseded**. A child graph refines inherited nodes; child states remain
    valid under inherited category edges. The final contract expresses this as
    contained graph refinement, not a serialized state-object merge scheme.

36. **Question:** How is creation's initial state selected without an entry
    field?
    **Answer:** Each resolved work-item lifecycle graph has exactly one
    plan-category root with no inbound lifecycle edge. Creation starts there.

37. **Question:** How are category labels determined for tunnel edges?
    **Answer:** Every resolved node carries its inherited base category; an edge

    **Answer:** Within-category edges, `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`,
    `verify -> act` for rework, and `act -> plan` for replanning. No skips.

39. **Question:** How does cancellation fit the universal lifecycle?
    **Answer:** Final answer: cancellation is a derived `verify` terminal leaf
    with no outgoing edge. It is the sole exception that may be entered directly
    from any lifecycle category.

40. **Question:** What is a terminal state?
    **Answer:** A resolved lifecycle node with no outgoing transition.

41. **Question:** What names distinguish state changes from ticket links?
    **Answer:** `lifecycle graph` for directed schema state transitions and
    `relation graph` for ticket links such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and
    remediation relations.

42. **Question:** Do relation edges have lifecycle-category constraints?
    **Answer:** No. Relation edges may cross ticket types and categories freely;
    validation applies declared relation-kind rules and endpoint existence.

43. **Question:** When do parent/cycle/type-ID failures occur?
    **Answer:** During explicit whole-registry load or reload; a failure retains
    the prior valid generation.

44. **Question:** What invalidates resolved schema caches?
    **Answer:** Content hash changes to a schema source or ancestor, checked on

45. **Question:** Is cache invalidation atomic?
    **Answer:** Yes. Registry generation, schema cache, manifest/catalog, and

    **Answer:** `model_version`, `sources`, `schemas`, and `graphs`; schema

    **Answer:** TOML and JSON deserialize through a shared model; CI fixture

    **Answer:** No. They are exempt until their individual Track 5 migration.

    **Answer:** All legacy records created before the model-version cutover.

    **Answer:** Only legacy `task` and `tracker-improvement` tickets.

    **Answer:** Targets are `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`,

    **Answer:** Only a unique top score of at least 0.80. Ties at any score,

    no timeout or default.

59. **Question:** How are classifier and approval results stored?
    **Answer:** In immutable migration parts recording classifier version,
    candidate scores, selected target, rules, explanation, and approval.

60. **Question:** How are concurrent decisions resolved?
    **Answer:** The latest approved immutable decision part is authoritative;
    conflicting pending parts block migration.

61. **Question:** Does the feature classifier use score-based migration?
    **Answer:** No. Legacy `feature` tickets use only the deterministic feature
    conversion table.

62. **Question:** What is the legacy feature conversion table?
    **Answer:** An active linked child/dependency creates an epic. Unchecked
    acceptance criteria alone create an implementation ticket. Both conditions
    create an epic. Neither creates an archived spec.

63. **Question:** How are corrective migrations represented?
    **Answer:** Original migration parts remain immutable. Track 6 appends a

    **Answer:** Roll back the affected transactional batch. Batches are
    idempotent and dry-run before live application.

65. **Question:** When does Track 5 end?
    **Answer:** After all approved batches commit and a migration-completion
    record is written.

66. **Question:** What does Track 6 do after Track 5 completion?
    **Answer:** Validate all evidence, block the entire release on any failing

    live-cutover, and remediation authorization tests; Playwright client tests;

verdict: pass
findings: []

- Persist and enforce the one-corrective-retry limit.
- Define the terminal handling of a rejected remediation review decision.

    **Answer:** No. Relation edges may cross ticket types and categories freely;

    **Answer:** Yes. Registry generation, schema cache, manifest/catalog, and

   templates. **Superseded** later by runtime inheritance.

3. **Question:** How much lifecycle enforcement should each concrete ticket
   type receive?

   `review`, to avoid conflict with the `review` ticket type.

4. **Question:** How should TOML and JSON schema files coexist?

   support for external/custom TOML and JSON. Shipped built-ins convert to JSON.

5. **Question:** What should phase-one migration do with existing records?

   Track 5 live migration contract.

6. **Question:** Which implementation tracks should be created?
   **Answer:** Initially five linked tracks. **Superseded** by six tracks after
   the engine/inheritance work became an explicit prerequisite.

7. **Question:** May any ticket bypass the universal lifecycle?

### First roast follow-ups

8. **Question:** How should inventory gate client defaults and type pickers?
   **Answer:** No inventory gate; client/default integration may proceed before

9. **Question:** How should directed lifecycle categories preserve legacy
   tickets?

   migration.

10. **Question:** Must duplicate diagnostics be deterministic?
    **Answer:** Yes. Sort paths and report collisions deterministically.

11. **Question:** Where should global directed transition/category migration
    live?
    **Answer:** A separate sixth prerequisite track.

12. **Question:** Can a ticket return from verification to work for rework?
    **Answer:** Yes: explicit `verify -> act -> verify` lifecycle loop.

13. **Question:** How should legacy schemas be handled by the global engine?
    **Answer:** Initially selected exemption from category enforcement until
    type migration. **Final:** the whole pre-cutover legacy cohort suspends
    workflow checks until individual migration.

14. **Question:** Who produces TOML and JSON artifacts?
    **Answer:** Initially decided JSON-only. **Superseded** by JSON shipped
    built-ins plus permanently supported custom TOML/JSON inputs.

15. **Question:** Should duplicate diagnostics list every collision?
    **Answer:** Yes, all colliding paths in lexical order.

16. **Question:** How should `review` type be distinguished from lifecycle
    category?
    **Answer:** Rename the lifecycle category to `verify`.

17. **Question:** Are epics exempt from the universal lifecycle?
    **Answer:** No. An epic traverses all categories; its `act` is orchestration
    and dependency coordination.

### Cutover and migration decisions

18. **Question:** Are duplicate type IDs fatal?
    **Answer:** Yes. Every duplicate type ID is a full registry-load error.

19. **Question:** How does directed enforcement apply to historical legacy
    transitions?
    **Answer:** Prospectively only, anchored by the shared manifest
    `model_version` cutover. Old history is unchanged and grandfathered.

20. **Question:** Does Track 5 execute live migration?
    **Answer:** Yes. Track 5 inventories, maps, dry-runs, executes idempotent
    transactional batches, removes exemptions, and writes a completion record.

21. **Question:** How do migrated legacy records satisfy universal lifecycle
    evidence?
    **Answer:** Their pre-cutover history is grandfathered; subsequent
    transitions follow the new rules.

22. **Question:** What is the required track order?
    **Answer:** Final sequence: engine/inheritance, dual loader, catalog and
    shipped JSON conversion, clients, migration, validation.

23. **Question:** Are shipped built-ins all converted before conversion
    cutover?
    **Answer:** Yes. Every shipped ticket built-in is converted to JSON;
    built-in TOML sources are deleted in catalog/conversion work.

24. **Question:** What happens to existing `bug` and `epic` IDs?
    **Answer:** Retain IDs and upgrade their schemas and active states in place,
    subject to global preflight.

25. **Question:** Does the directed engine apply only to tickets?
    **Answer:** No. Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse shared
    directed primitives but define local lifecycle graphs.

26. **Question:** Which rule schemas are included?
    **Answer:** Existing rule-api schemas such as `rule-entry` and
    `generated-target`; no new rule entity is introduced.

27. **Question:** When must the dual loader exist relative to shipped TOML
    deletion?
    **Answer:** The dual loader lands before built-in TOML sources are deleted.

28. **Question:** How should external custom TOML schemas work?
    **Answer:** They remain permanently supported alongside custom JSON.

29. **Question:** May custom schemas override built-ins?
    **Answer:** No. Any collision, including built-in/custom, is fatal.

30. **Question:** What is the duplicate-ID namespace?
    **Answer:** Type IDs are unique per schema kind; ticket, spec, and rule
    registries have separate namespaces.

### Runtime inheritance and lifecycle graph decisions

31. **Question:** Should inheritance return to the design?
    **Answer:** Yes. Runtime inheritance resolves derived schemas dynamically
    and caches unchanged resolved schemas for low-latency use.

32. **Question:** What parent topology is allowed?
    **Answer:** Strict zero-or-one parent, linear parent chains only; missing
    parents and cycles fail.

33. **Question:** How should derived states relate to base lifecycle states?
    **Answer:** A derived schema refines inherited lifecycle nodes into contained
    subgraphs or tunnels. Resolved nodes retain inherited base-category labels.

34. **Question:** How does a transition enter a derived category tunnel?
    **Answer:** A transition explicitly names a concrete target state; the
    resolver validates the resolved concrete edge and inherited category pair.

35. **Question:** How should child state-object overrides work?
    **Answer:** Earlier field-wise merge and explicit entry-flag options were
    **superseded**. A child graph refines inherited nodes; child states remain
    valid under inherited category edges. The final contract expresses this as
    contained graph refinement, not a serialized state-object merge scheme.

36. **Question:** How is creation's initial state selected without an entry
    field?
    **Answer:** Each resolved work-item lifecycle graph has exactly one
    plan-category root with no inbound lifecycle edge. Creation starts there.

37. **Question:** How are category labels determined for tunnel edges?
    **Answer:** Every resolved node carries its inherited base category; an edge
    is validated using its source/target category pair.

38. **Question:** Which normal lifecycle transitions are legal?
    **Answer:** Within-category edges, `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`,
    `verify -> act` for rework, and `act -> plan` for replanning. No skips.

39. **Question:** How does cancellation fit the universal lifecycle?
    **Answer:** Final answer: cancellation is a derived `verify` terminal leaf
    with no outgoing edge. It is the sole exception that may be entered directly
    from any lifecycle category.

40. **Question:** What is a terminal state?
    **Answer:** A resolved lifecycle node with no outgoing transition.

41. **Question:** What names distinguish state changes from ticket links?
    **Answer:** `lifecycle graph` for directed schema state transitions and
    `relation graph` for ticket links such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and
    remediation relations.

42. **Question:** Do relation edges have lifecycle-category constraints?
    **Answer:** No. Relation edges may cross ticket types and categories freely;
    validation applies declared relation-kind rules and endpoint existence.

### Registry, manifest, and reload decisions

43. **Question:** When do parent/cycle/type-ID failures occur?
    **Answer:** During explicit whole-registry load or reload; a failure retains
    the prior valid generation.

44. **Question:** What invalidates resolved schema caches?
    **Answer:** Content hash changes to a schema source or ancestor, checked on
    explicit reload.

45. **Question:** Is cache invalidation atomic?
    **Answer:** Yes. Registry generation, schema cache, manifest/catalog, and
    client cache version commit together or the prior generation remains.

46. **Question:** What does the generated registry manifest contain?
    **Answer:** `model_version`, `sources`, `schemas`, and `graphs`; schema
    records have IDs, parent chains, hashes, resolved nodes/transitions/
    terminals, and type metadata; graph records name entity kind and schema IDs.

47. **Question:** How is format parity enforced?
    **Answer:** TOML and JSON deserialize through a shared model; CI fixture

48. **Question:** How are duplicate diagnostic paths ordered?
    **Answer:** Sort the union of all eligible TOML and JSON paths lexically,

    **Answer:** A reviewer may select remediation instead. A typed

    **Answer:** The canonical-type upgrade and the whole release are blocked.

52. **Question:** Are pre-model active tickets subject to this preflight?
    **Answer:** No. They are exempt until their individual Track 5 migration.

53. **Question:** Which records are the legacy exemption cohort?
    **Answer:** All legacy records created before the model-version cutover.

    evidence is grandfathered.

54. **Question:** When does a legacy record leave the exemption cohort?
    **Answer:** Only when a committed, approved Track 5 migration batch writes

    **Answer:** Preserve and resume the ticket's last non-on-hold lifecycle

    **Answer:** Only legacy `task` and `tracker-improvement` tickets.

    **Answer:** Targets are `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`,

    and relation edges. A Track 5 research sub-ticket defines concrete rules,
    weights, and tie calculation.

    **Answer:** Only a unique top score of at least 0.80. Ties at any score,
    lower scores, and missing scores require linked review-ticket approval with
    no timeout or default.

59. **Question:** How are classifier and approval results stored?
    **Answer:** In immutable migration parts recording classifier version,
    candidate scores, selected target, rules, explanation, and approval.

60. **Question:** How are concurrent decisions resolved?
    **Answer:** The latest approved immutable decision part is authoritative;
    conflicting pending parts block migration.

61. **Question:** Does the feature classifier use score-based migration?
    **Answer:** No. Legacy `feature` tickets use only the deterministic feature
    conversion table.

62. **Question:** What is the legacy feature conversion table?
    **Answer:** An active linked child/dependency creates an epic. Unchecked
    acceptance criteria alone create an implementation ticket. Both conditions
    create an epic. Neither creates an archived spec.

63. **Question:** How are corrective migrations represented?
    **Answer:** Original migration parts remain immutable. Track 6 appends a
    new immutable `corrective-migration` part linked by `supersedes`, recording
    the remediation review decision and current-state mapping. The latest
    approved superseding corrective part is authoritative.

### Release, repair, and validation decisions

64. **Question:** What does a Track 5 batch failure do?
    **Answer:** Roll back the affected transactional batch. Batches are
    idempotent and dry-run before live application.

65. **Question:** When does Track 5 end?
    **Answer:** After all approved batches commit and a migration-completion
    record is written.

66. **Question:** What does Track 6 do after Track 5 completion?
    **Answer:** Validate all evidence, block the entire release on any failing
    validation or forward-repair batch, never roll back completed batches or
    restore exemptions, and repair forward using new transactional corrective
    migration batches from current state.

67. **Question:** How many corrective retries are allowed?
    **Answer:** One repaired retry. A second failure keeps release blocked and
    requires a human-approved remediation review ticket before corrective work
    may continue.

68. **Question:** What validation evidence is required?
    **Answer:** Focused unit/contract tests; CLI/MCP/HTTP parity; TOML/JSON
    resolved-manifest fixture parity; migration dry-run, idempotence, rollback,
    live-cutover, and remediation authorization tests; Playwright client tests;
    and an all-pass Track 6 matrix.

## Final Review

The final Roast Agent reviewed the completed contract and returned:

```text
verdict: pass
findings: []
```

The final Roast Agent identified residual implementation risks to capture in
future acceptance criteria, not unresolved design decisions:

- Enforce selection of the latest approved `supersedes` chain.
- Persist and enforce the one-corrective-retry limit.
- Define the terminal handling of a rejected remediation review decision.

    explicit reload.

This file records the full interview conducted after the initial review of
[input.clean.md](input.clean.md). Entries are chronological. A decision marked
**Superseded** was replaced by a later answer and is not part of the final
planning contract.

## Final Planning Contract

- Feature functionality is represented by specs, not ticket types.
- New work-item ticket types are `epic`, `bug`, `research`, `planning`,
  `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`.
- `task`, `feature`, and `tracker-improvement` are legacy ticket types until
  their individual Track 5 migrations.
- Schemas use strict, runtime, single-parent inheritance beneath a universal
  work-item schema. Resolved schemas are dynamically generated and cached.
- The universal work-item lifecycle categories are `plan`, `act`, and
  `verify`. Every concrete work-item type refines one or more nodes in each
  category and has at least one valid path across all three categories.
- A schema's directed state-transition structure is the **lifecycle graph**.
  Ticket links such as `depends_on`, `linked`, and
  `remediation_approved_by` form the **relation graph**.
- Derived schemas refine inherited lifecycle nodes into category-contained
  subgraphs. A resolved node retains the inherited category label. Edges may
  remain within a category or cross only between neighbouring category edges:
  `plan -> act`, `act -> verify`, `verify -> act` for rework, and
  `act -> plan` for replanning. No normal lifecycle skips are permitted.
- Each resolved work-item schema has exactly one plan-category root with no
  inbound lifecycle edge; creation begins there. Every transition names a
  concrete target state and is validated against the resolved lifecycle graph.
- Cancellation is a derived `verify` terminal leaf. It is the sole exception
  that may be reached directly from any lifecycle category. Terminal nodes
  have no outgoing edges.
- Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse shared directed lifecycle
  primitives while maintaining separate local graphs and separate type-ID
  namespaces.
- Schema inheritance is linear: zero or one parent; missing parents and cycles
  are rejected. Parent/cycle/type-ID validation occurs during an explicit,
  atomic load or reload. A failed reload retains the last valid registry.
- On explicit reload, source and ancestor content hashes invalidate affected
  resolved-schema cache entries, resolved manifests, catalog indexes, and
  client cache versions atomically.
- The typed resolved-registry manifest includes `model_version`, `sources`,
  `schemas`, and `graphs`. Schema records include IDs, parent chains, hashes,
  resolved nodes, transitions, terminals, and type metadata. Graph records
  name their entity kind and schema IDs.
- Shipped ticket schemas become JSON sources. External/custom schema directories
  permanently support both TOML and JSON through a shared model/parser.
  Built-in and custom schemas share one combined lexical path sort. Any
  duplicate type ID within one schema kind, including a built-in/custom
  collision, rejects the complete load and reports every colliding path in
  lexical order. Custom schemas cannot override built-ins. CI compares
  equivalent TOML/JSON fixtures by resolved manifest.
- Tracks are ordered: 1. engine/inheritance, 2. dual-format loader,
  3. generated catalog and shipped-ticket JSON conversion, 4. CLI and VS Code
  clients, 5. migration, 6. release validation.
- `bug` and `epic` retain their canonical IDs. Their schemas and active states
  upgrade in place only after global preflight. Active means `open`, `planned`,
  `in-implementation`, `in-review`, or `on-hold`. Each active record needs a
  direct lifecycle route or reviewer-selected remediation approved by a typed
  `remediation_approved_by` relation edge to a review ticket with an immutable
  decision part. Missing proof blocks the canonical-type upgrade and the whole
  release. Pre-model active records are exempt until individual migration.

  the model cutover are one exemption cohort: workflow checks are suspended
  until the individual record is migrated, prior history is grandfathered, and
  the first transition after migration follows the new model. A legacy
  `on-hold` record preserves its last non-on-hold lifecycle category.

  weights and ties for `task` and `tracker-improvement`, using title,
  description, fields, state, and relation edges against targets `research`,
  `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`. Only a
  unique top score of at least 0.80 auto-migrates. Tied, lower, and missing
  scores require a linked review-ticket decision, with no timeout or default.

  state. One corrective retry is allowed. A second failure keeps the release
  blocked until a human-approved remediation review ticket exists.

  `supersedes` the original immutable migration part and records the review
  decision and current-state mapping. The latest approved superseding
  corrective part is authoritative for future validation.

The Track‑6 contract in `transcripts/05-08-2026_ticketschema-state-machines/interview.md` says one corrective retry is allowed and a second failure “blocks release until a human‑approved remediation review ticket exists”; it is silent about what to do if that remediation review then rejects the corrective work — which behavior should we adopt?

Option A — Require a new remediation review ticket before any further corrective batch:
- Observable consequences: the original remediation ticket is marked `rejected`; CI/gates refuse any corrective batch that references the rejected ticket; a new remediation ticket (new id) must be created and human‑approved before the pipeline accepts another corrective batch; release remains blocked; all completed batches and immutable evidence remain recorded and unrolled.
Option B — Allow iterative rework under the same remediation review ticket:
- Observable consequences: the remediation ticket stays open with status `rework`/`iteration`; reviewers annotate rejection with required fixes but do not close the ticket; CI/gates accept new corrective batches that reference the same remediation ticket id (each recorded as a new idempotent forward repair); release remains blocked until an approval is recorded; completed batches and immutable evidence remain recorded and unrolled.
Recommended default: Option A — require a new remediation review ticket (ensures a fresh, auditable approval cycle and avoids indefinite reopen/reject loops).

arguments.content:
## Normative Record

The binding source is [Ticket Schema Modernization Interview](transcripts/05-08-2026_ticketschema-state-machines/interview.md); superseded interview answers are non-normative.

- `cancelled` is a derived `verify` terminal leaf with no outgoing lifecycle edge. It is the sole direct-entry exception from any lifecycle category.
- The resolved manifest contains top-level `model_version`, `sources`, `schemas`, and `graphs`. Schema records include IDs, parent chains, hashes, resolved nodes, transitions, terminals, and type metadata. Graph records declare entity kind and schema IDs.
- Ticket, spec, and existing rule schemas reuse shared directed-lifecycle primitives but keep independent local graphs and separate type-ID namespaces. Relation edges validate declared relation-kind rules and endpoint existence only; lifecycle constraints never apply to relation edges.
- `bug` and `epic` preserve canonical IDs and upgrade in place only after global preflight. An active record is `open`, `planned`, `in-implementation`, `in-review`, or `on-hold`; it needs either a direct lifecycle route or a typed `remediation_approved_by` relation to a review ticket with an immutable approval decision. Missing proof blocks upgrade and release.
- Current manifest rules govern a transition. All records created before model-version cutover are a workflow-exempt cohort: prior history is grandfathered, checks suspend until individual migration, and the first post-migration transition follows the current model. `on-hold` restores the last non-on-hold category.
- A Track 5 research child defines deterministic rules-first classifier weights and ties for legacy `task` and `tracker-improvement`, using title, description, fields, state, and relation edges. Targets are `research`, `planning`, `implementation`, `review`, `interview`, and `testing`. Only a unique score of at least `0.80` auto-migrates; ties, lower/missing scores, and conflicting pending decisions require linked review approval with no timeout/default. Immutable evidence records classifier version, candidates, scores, rule explanation, selected target, and approval. The latest approved immutable decision is authoritative.
- Legacy `feature` conversion is deterministic: active child/dependency -> epic; unchecked acceptance criteria only -> implementation; both -> epic; neither -> archived spec.
- Track 5 writes a migration-completion record only after approved idempotent transactional batches commit.
- Track 6 begins only after Track 5 completion, blocks release on any failed validation/corrective batch, and requires an all-pass validation matrix. Corrective parts are immutable and follow the latest approved `supersedes` chain. One corrective retry is permitted; after a second failure, a human-approved remediation review is required. A rejected remediation review closes that approval path and requires a new remediation review ticket and fresh human approval before another corrective batch. Release remains blocked throughout; completed batches are never rolled back.

content.objective: Deliver an implementation-ready handoff for the schema-modernization Track‑1 first slice: implement strict single-parent runtime inheritance and a directed plan/act/verify lifecycle graph (single plan root, declared normal/rework/replan edges, `cancelled` as a derived verify terminal/sole direct-entry exception), separate lifecycle vs relation graphs and namespaces, atomic reload/generation/cache invalidation, and a small focused test-suite plus the policy rule that links the owning spec to the runtime guard.
decisions: Single-parent runtime inheritance model: each runtime instance inherits from exactly one parent schema at runtime; no multi-parent merge for this slice.

Lifecycle graph separation: lifecycle (plan → act → verify) is modelled as a directed graph with exactly one declared plan root; relation/aux graphs live in a separate namespace and do not carry lifecycle transitions.

Edge kinds declared explicitly: implement `normal`, `rework`, and `replan` edge types in the lifecycle graph data model and manifest. Consumers must treat `rework` as in-place re-validate and `replan` as branch + new plan root semantics.
`cancelled` is a derived verify-terminal: allow direct-entry only as a documented, narrow exception; other direct entries to verify must be rejected.

Atomic reload/generation/cache invalidation: registry reload and any generated artifacts update must be atomic with a single in-process swap and coordinated cache invalidation accessible via `SchemaRegistry` APIs; no half-applied state allowed.

Policy link: the owning spec (e9c38d24-42cc-4044-8b2c-6811b918530f) will provide the guard/policy rule artifact; the runtime enforces the guard through the registry-level validation hook rather than ad‑hoc checks scattered across store code.

Tests-first contract: focused unit and integration tests are required to cover schema parsing, registry lookup semantics, single-parent inheritance resolution, lifecycle graph invariants, atomic reload behavior, and rule-schema integration smoke.
validation: Run crate tests: `rtk cargo test -p memory-api`
Run ticket-api tests: `rtk cargo test -p ticket-api`
Run spec-api focused test: `rtk cargo test -p spec-api` (verifies `spec_schema_registry` and spec guard contract)
Run rule-api focused test: `rtk cargo test -p rule-api` (verifies rule-schema registry and rule-loading smoke)

Focused checks after implementation: (a) unit tests that assert single-parent inheritance resolution returns the single ancestor and rejects multiple-parent inputs; (b) unit/integration tests that exercise `SchemaRegistry` reload and confirm no stale handles remain; (c) lifecycle graph invariants tests: single plan root, explicit edge kinds, `cancelled` terminal behavior; (d) a rule-schema integration smoke that loads the guard from spec e9c38d24 and validates it against the registry.
non_goals: Dual-format loader (do not implement dual TOML/JSON schema loading in this slice).
Manifest/catalog JSON built-in exporters or new catalog CLI/VSCode integration.
Classifier/heuristic research for automapping old manifests — migration tooling is out-of-scope.
Large data migrations, cross-track migrations, or Track‑6 release work.

Spec tests: memory-api/crates/spec-api/tests/schema_test.rs (adjacent focused test module to mirror expected behaviours)
risk_notes: Back-compat risk: enforcing strict single-parent semantics may cause existing manifests (or test fixtures) that implicitly relied on merging to fail; plan for one-off fixture updates and a clear compatibility story if needed.

Atomic reload concurrency: if other threads hold references into the previous `SchemaRegistry` internal structures, naive swap may produce races—design the swap to use an `Arc`-based replace and validate no long-lived mutable references remain.
Rule integration surprises: rule-api and ticket-api expect built-ins in slightly different shapes; include a smoke test to surface any shape mismatches early.

Test coverage gaps: missing focused tests in the ticket‑manifest validation path (manifest → `EntityTypeSchema` → lifecycle invariants) will allow regressions; ensure tests exercise the store code paths that call `SchemaRegistry` (store open, manifest validation, lifecycle transitions).

Performance/regeneration cost: registry generation and cache invalidation must be measured on representative fixtures; an atomic full-regenerate might be acceptable for this slice but could be too expensive at scale—document observed timings during implementation.

arguments.objective: Implement ticket 7ef3f8db: the shared directed inherited schema lifecycle engine, including the recovered full-interview requirements assigned to Track 1.
decisions: Strict runtime schema inheritance permits zero or one parent; missing parents and parent cycles reject the complete load/reload.

Lifecycle graphs are directed and use universal plan, act, and verify categories. Derived schemas refine inherited nodes only through category-contained subgraphs/tunnels and exactly one plan-category root starts creation.
Lifecycle edges may remain within a category or cross only plan-to-act, act-to-verify, verify-to-act rework, and act-to-plan replanning; no normal category skips are permitted.

arguments.name: Implementation Workflow and Role Mapping
arguments.content:
## Decision Record

The currently registered ticket schemas are legacy (`epic`, `bug`, `feature`, `task`, `tracker-improvement`). Until Track 3 installs the target schema catalog, workflow-role tickets use legacy `tracker-improvement` storage with explicit `target_schema_type` and `workflow_role` fields. This is a compatibility representation, not a semantic change.

- Epic [8fdfe135 Schema modernization implementation track](.ticket/tickets/8fdfe135-e3b1-4876-b638-24154edcd78d/ticket.toml) maps to target `epic`.
- Existing feature slices [7ef3f8db Implement directed inherited schema lifecycle engine](.ticket/tickets/7ef3f8db-d4a9-4135-99eb-3c006070a328/ticket.toml), [1f8e6e6d Add deterministic dual-format schema loading](.ticket/tickets/1f8e6e6d-c8a1-461d-83c9-c26daf0e3cd3/ticket.toml), [abd3f280 Generate resolved schema catalog and JSON built-ins](.ticket/tickets/abd3f280-9bd1-48cf-8503-17dd820afb30/ticket.toml), [9e7a5f1a Integrate schema catalog into CLI and VS Code](.ticket/tickets/9e7a5f1a-a2ce-43ce-9c8f-bdce7cf712d2/ticket.toml), and [7df984eb Inventory and migrate legacy ticket schemas](.ticket/tickets/7df984eb-c96c-4501-98fa-4e88dd28ec4e/ticket.toml) map to target `implementation`.
- [3bb41fb2 Validate schema modernization release and repair flow](.ticket/tickets/3bb41fb2-9907-4b54-83b1-c62a0ce96756/ticket.toml) maps to target `testing`; [e03eb731 Review schema modernization completion evidence](.ticket/tickets/e03eb731-877a-4498-832f-d1e41526423a/ticket.toml) maps to target `review`.
- Every implementation/testing slice is preceded by a role-mapped `research` ticket and a role-mapped `planning` ticket. Research produces a cited brief; planning converts the brief and binding decision register into target files, acceptance criteria, validation commands, and scope boundaries. No implementation/testing ticket begins before its planning dependency is done.
- The complete execution chain is lifecycle-engine research -> lifecycle-engine planning -> engine implementation -> loader research -> loader planning -> loader implementation -> catalog research -> catalog planning -> catalog implementation -> client research -> client planning -> client implementation -> classifier research -> migration planning -> migration implementation -> release research -> release planning -> release testing -> completion review.
- Research, planning, implementation, testing, and review are distinct target roles. Their current shared legacy storage type must be replaced by their target schema types only through the Track 3 catalog and Track 5 migration contracts.

## Acceptance Record
The epic closes only after each role-mapped ticket is complete, every implementation handoff cites its preceding research/planning records, Track 6 validation passes, and the review ticket approves the final evidence.
